S1.q: Is this person-to-person only, or do people also pay businesses?
S1.decides: Merchant onboarding, seller fees, refunds, chargebacks and tax reporting all appear or vanish.

S2.q: Do users hold a balance inside the app, or does every payment go straight from bank to bank?
S2.decides: Whether a wallet and ledger are the system of record, what licences are needed, and whether cash-out exists.

S3.q: Which ways in and out at launch: bank transfer, debit card, credit card, instant payout?
S3.decides: Which rails are integrated, how long settlement takes, and what each payment costs.

S4.q: Is the social feed (who paid whom, comments, likes) part of the first version?
S4.decides: A whole feed subsystem and its privacy model.

S5.q: Beyond "send": requests, bill splitting, recurring or scheduled payments?
S5.decides: A scheduler and multi-step payment state.

S6.q: What is explicitly not in the first version: cards, crypto, credit, cross-border, accounts for minors?
S6.decides: The non-goals list, and several licences.

M1.q: Who legally holds customer money: us under our own licences, or a partner bank on our behalf?
M1.decides: Whether our ledger or the partner's is the record of truth, how much the partner's API dictates, and the launch timeline.

M2.q: Which countries, states and currencies at launch?
M2.decides: Licensing per jurisdiction, currency conversion, data residency and per-region rules.

M3.q: What can an unverified user do, and what triggers identity verification?
M3.decides: Sign-up friction, limit tiers, and whether the identity vendor sits in the sign-up path or later.

M4.q: Who absorbs fraud and unauthorised-payment losses: us, the partner, or the user?
M4.decides: How much risk decisioning sits in the payment path, how long funds are held, and how much dispute tooling is built.

M5.q: Sanctions screening and transaction monitoring: bought or built, and does it block the payment or run after it?
M5.decides: A synchronous call in the payment path against an asynchronous pipeline with case management.

M6.q: What reporting and record-keeping is required: tax forms for sellers, suspicious-activity reports, retention period, card-data security scope?
M6.decides: Compliance reporting, immutable history, and whether a vendor tokenises card data to keep it out of our systems.

P1.q: Who is the launch customer: friends splitting costs, people getting paid for work or goods, or one specific community such as a campus or a marketplace?
P1.decides: Which flows are core and how network density is built.

P2.q: Can you pay someone who has no account yet?
P2.decides: Pending payments, a claim flow, expiry and refund, and unclaimed money.

P3.q: Is there a seller or business profile with different rules for fees, buyer protection and tax?
P3.decides: Account types, the fee model and refunds.

P4.q: Which internal roles need tooling on day one: support, risk and compliance, finance?
P4.decides: How much back office is in the first build.

P5.q: For each persona, when is a payment "done": when the sender sees success, or when the receiver can spend or withdraw it?
P5.decides: Instant availability, and with it how much money the company fronts.

C1.q: Is a sent payment final, or can it be cancelled or reversed? By whom, and for how long?
C1.decides: The payment state machine, reversal entries and what support staff may do.

C2.q: What happens when a bank pull fails after the receiver already has the money?
C2.decides: Negative balances, clawback, collections and hold periods.

C3.q: What must happen on a double tap, a retry, or a timeout from the bank?
C3.decides: Idempotency keys, handling of unknown outcomes, and reconciliation.

C4.q: What must be exactly right immediately (the balance), and what may lag (feed, notifications, analytics)?
C4.decides: Strong or eventual consistency, component by component.

C5.q: How are disputes and "I did not make this payment" claims handled, and how fast?
C5.decides: Case management and provisional-credit entries in the ledger.

C6.q: What is the default visibility of a payment: public, friends only, or private?
C6.decides: The feed's privacy model. Hard to change later without losing trust.

B1.q: How many users, payments per day and dollars per day at launch and in three years?
B1.decides: One database or a partitioned ledger. One of the few places arithmetic picks the design.

B2.q: What do peaks look like: rent day, weekends, holidays?
B2.decides: Queue buffering, capacity, and whether partner rate limits bind.

B3.q: What are the typical and maximum payment sizes, and the weekly limits?
B3.decides: Loss exposure per account and the risk tiers.

B4.q: How much money can the company front? If the receiver gets funds instantly but the bank pull settles days later, we are lending.
B4.decides: Instant against delayed availability, and hold rules.

B5.q: What does an hour of downtime cost, and may payments queue when a rail or partner is down?
B5.decides: Redundancy, a second partner, and a degraded mode.

G1.q: What is the growth loop: paying non-users, contact matching, QR codes, the public feed, referral bonuses?
G1.decides: An invites service, contact upload and its privacy handling, and the claim flow.

G2.q: What is the activation moment, and how little can we ask for before it? Can someone send before linking a bank, or before identity checks?

G3.q: Where does revenue come from: instant cash-out fee, card funding fee, seller fee, card interchange, interest on balances?
G3.decides: The fee model, revenue accounts in the ledger, and pricing configuration.

G4.q: Are there sign-up or referral rewards?
G4.decides: Promotional balances in the ledger and detection of fake-account farming.

G5.q: What must be testable as an experiment: fees, onboarding steps, limits?

K1.q: Which rules must change without a release (limits, fees, hold periods, risk thresholds), and along which dimensions (verification tier, region, funding source, cohort)?
K1.decides: A policy engine against hard-coded rules.

K2.q: Who may change those rules, and what approval and audit trail is required?
K2.decides: A configuration console with two-person approval and an audit log.

K3.q: What can users set: privacy default, notification preferences, default funding source, automatic cash-out, app lock?
K3.decides: A settings store that is read on the payment path.

K4.q: Will there be more than one bank partner or processor, with routing rules between them?
K4.decides: A rails abstraction, per-partner configuration and failover.

K5.q: Is this one app, or a platform other companies embed under their own brand?
K5.decides: Multi-tenancy, a partner API and a full control plane.

T1.q: Is anything mandated: cloud, languages, datastores, client platforms, or existing systems to integrate such as a current user base?

T2.q: Which vendors are already contracted: bank partner, processor, identity verification, fraud?
T2.decides: Their APIs and limits shape the design more than our preferences do.

T3.q: How large is the team, what must launch by what date, and what is the stance on building or buying the ledger, identity checks and fraud?
T3.decides: One deployable or several services, and which parts are vendor-backed.

T4.q: What do auditors and partners require of the stack itself: card-data scope, encryption and key management, change control, data residency?
T4.decides: Network segmentation, vendor tokenisation and the deployment process.

U1.q: Who reconciles our ledger against the bank's records every day, and what happens when they disagree?
U1.decides: A reconciliation job, a break queue and a finance console.

U2.q: What are the cut-offs and return windows on each rail, including weekends, holidays and late returns?
U2.decides: Hold periods and when funds are truly final.

U3.q: What happens to unclaimed payments, dormant balances, and the accounts of users who close, die, or are frozen by court order?
U3.decides: Account states, scheduled sweeps and legal processes.

U4.q: What if the bank partner changes its limits, has an outage, or ends the relationship?
U4.decides: Whether accounts and the ledger can be moved to another partner.

U5.q: Card-funded payments can be charged back months later. Who pays?
U5.decides: Reserves, seller holds and the dispute workflow.

U6.q: Financial records must be kept for years, and privacy law lets users ask for deletion. Which wins where?
U6.decides: Separation of personal data from ledger records.

U7.q: How is a wrong ledger entry corrected, and how are balances migrated or backfilled?
U7.decides: An append-only ledger with reversing entries, and migration tooling.

nodes.label: Sender
nodes.what: Someone paying another person.
nodes.expects: Finds the right person fast, the payment feels instant, mistakes can be undone, and it is free.

nodes.label: Receiver
nodes.what: Someone on the receiving end.
nodes.expects: Money is usable straight away and can be moved to a bank quickly.

nodes.label: Invited non-user
nodes.what: A person who is sent money or a request and has no account.
nodes.expects: Claims the money in a minute or two without a long sign-up.

nodes.label: Seller or business
nodes.what: Someone accepting payment for goods or work.
nodes.expects: Proof of payment, clear fees, refunds, tax documents.

options.name: Person-to-person only
options.when: the launch customer is friends splitting costs

options.name: Business profiles
options.when: people are already using it to get paid and that is where revenue is

nodes.label: Support agent
nodes.what: Handles "wrong person", "did not arrive" and scam reports.
nodes.expects: Sees a payment end to end and can act within clear limits.

nodes.label: Risk and compliance
nodes.what: Reviews flagged accounts and payments.
nodes.expects: A queue of cases, the evidence for each, and the power to freeze.

nodes.label: Finance operations
nodes.what: Makes sure our books match the bank's.
nodes.expects: A daily view of what did not match and why.

nodes.label: Mobile and web apps
nodes.what: Everything a customer touches.

nodes.label: API gateway
nodes.what: The single way in for clients. Every money-moving call carries an idempotency key so a retry is recognised.

fork.q: Our own apps only, or a platform others embed?

options.name: First-party API
options.when: one brand, one set of rules

options.name: Partner platform
options.when: other companies offer payments under their own brand, which makes the system multi-tenant

nodes.label: Back-office console
nodes.what: One place for support, risk and finance staff. Access is bounded by role and every action is logged.

nodes.label: Identity and onboarding
nodes.what: Creates accounts, verifies who people are, binds devices.

fork.q: Verify identity up front, or progressively?

options.name: Up front
options.when: the partner or regulator requires it before any money moves

options.name: Progressive tiers
options.when: activation matters most and small unverified limits are allowed

nodes.label: Payments orchestrator
nodes.sub: send, cancel, reverse; state per payment
nodes.what: Owns the life of a payment: checks, ledger posting, funding pull, completion or failure.

nodes.label: Requests, splits, scheduled
nodes.what: Anything beyond a plain send. Each adds states and, for scheduled payments, a timer.

nodes.label: Social feed
nodes.what: A stream of who paid whom, with comments and likes. Built from payment events, never from the ledger directly.

fork.q: Is the feed in the first version, and what is visible by default?

options.name: No feed
options.when: the product is a utility

options.name: Feed, private by default
options.when: trust matters more than virality

options.name: Feed, public by default
options.when: the feed is the growth loop

nodes.label: Growth and invites
nodes.what: Finds people you know, lets you pay people who have not joined, and pays out rewards.

nodes.label: Disputes and cases
nodes.what: Tracks every claim to an outcome within a deadline.
nodes.note: Consumer-protection rules and card-network rules set the deadlines and who is out of pocket meanwhile.

nodes.label: Wallet and balances
nodes.what: What each user has available to spend or withdraw. A view over the ledger.

options.name: Stored balance
options.when: receivers should be able to re-spend at once and cash out later

options.name: Pass-through
options.when: holding customer money is to be avoided and every payment settles bank to bank

nodes.label: Double-entry ledger
nodes.what: The record of truth for money. Entries are never edited; corrections are new entries.

fork.q: Is our ledger the record of truth, or the partner's?

options.name: Own ledger
options.when: we hold licences, or want to be able to change partner

options.name: Partner's ledger with a local mirror
options.when: speed to launch matters most and the partner already provides accounts

nodes.label: Funding and payout rails
nodes.sub: which rails? one partner or several?
nodes.what: Pulls money in and pushes it out through banks and card networks.

fork.q: Which rails, and how many providers?

options.name: Bank transfer only, one provider
options.when: cost per payment must be near zero and days of delay are acceptable

options.name: Cards and instant payout too
options.when: instant is the product, and fees or revenue cover the cost

options.name: Several providers with routing
options.when: an outage or a lost partner would be fatal

nodes.label: Risk decision
nodes.sub: in the payment path, or after it?
nodes.what: Approve, hold or decline each payment and each sign-up.

fork.q: Block in the payment path, or review afterwards?

options.name: Synchronous decision
options.when: we carry the loss and money leaves instantly

options.name: Asynchronous review
options.when: funds are held before release anyway, or the partner carries the loss

nodes.label: Limits and fees
nodes.what: Applies sending limits and works out any fee before the ledger is touched.

nodes.label: Policy and configuration
nodes.sub: rules as data, or in code?
nodes.what: Holds limits, fees, hold periods, risk thresholds and flags. Changes are approved and written to an audit log.

fork.q: Hard-coded rules, or a rules store staff can change?

options.name: In code
options.when: one region, one tier, rules rarely change

options.name: Configurable
options.when: rules vary by region, tier and funding source, or will be tested as experiments

nodes.label: Event stream
nodes.sub: every ledger change is published once, in order, and can be replayed
nodes.what: Several independent consumers need each payment event, and some need to rebuild from history. An outbox guarantees an event follows every ledger write.

nodes.label: Settlement and reconciliation
nodes.what: Matches ledger entries to bank and processor files every day and queues what does not match.
nodes.note: Cut-off times, return windows and file formats are set by the rails and the partner.

nodes.label: Scheduler and jobs
nodes.what: Work driven by time: scheduled payments, expiry of unclaimed money, hold releases, statements.

nodes.label: Notifications
nodes.what: Tells people about money in, money out and requests. Also the channel that brings invited people in.

nodes.label: Compliance and tax reporting
nodes.what: Produces what regulators and tax authorities require from the ledger history.
nodes.note: Retention periods and report formats are fixed by law and differ by jurisdiction.

nodes.label: Transaction monitoring
nodes.what: Looks for suspicious patterns across payments and raises cases.
nodes.note: Anti-money-laundering obligations apply whoever holds the licence.

nodes.label: Analytics and experiments
nodes.what: Measures activation and the growth loop, and assigns users to experiments.

nodes.label: Identity verification vendor
nodes.what: Checks documents and identity data. Its response time sits inside sign-up.

nodes.label: Push, text and email providers
nodes.what: Third-party delivery. Slow or down at times, so it sits behind a queue.

nodes.label: Regulators and tax authority
nodes.what: Receive filings and can demand records.
nodes.note: Which ones apply depends on where we launch and who holds the licence.

nodes.label: Sanctions and watchlist data
nodes.what: Lists every customer and counterparty is screened against.
nodes.note: Screening is mandatory; only how and when is ours to decide.

nodes.label: Card and bank-transfer rails
nodes.what: The systems that move money between banks.
nodes.note: Each rail has its own speed, cost, cut-offs, return rules and security requirements.

nodes.label: Bank partner
nodes.what: Holds customer funds, or holds our operating accounts if we are licensed ourselves.
nodes.note: A sponsor can change limits or end the programme.

fork.q: Our own licences, or a sponsor bank?

options.name: Sponsor bank
options.when: launch speed matters and we accept its rules, limits and oversight

options.name: Own licences
options.when: control and margin justify a much longer path to launch
